question: What is REST and what makes an API RESTful?
title: What is REST – RESTful API Fundamentals for Java Developers
direct_answer: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for designing networked applications. An API is RESTful when it treats everything as a resource identified by URIs, uses standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to operate on those resources, and maintains statelessness—each request carries all needed context without server-side session storage.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand REST as architectural constraints, not just 'using HTTP for JSON APIs'
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling REST a protocol or specification—it's neither, it's an architectural style with principles
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Roy Fielding's dissertation and name at least three REST constraints: statelessness, uniform interface, client-server separation

sections.title: Understanding REST as an Architectural Style
sections.content:
**REST** (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style introduced by Roy Fielding in his 2000 doctoral dissertation.

Think of it like building codes for houses—REST doesn't tell you exactly how to build your API, but it gives you principles that make it scalable, maintainable, and predictable. An API is **RESTful** when it follows six key constraints: **client-server separation** (UI and backend evolve independently), **statelessness** (each request is self-contained), **cacheability** (responses label themselves as cacheable or not), **uniform interface** (consistent patterns for all resources), **layered system** (clients can't tell if they're talking to the end server or an intermediary), and **code on demand** (optional—server can send executable code). The WHY matters: these constraints enable horizontal scaling, simplify debugging, and let mobile apps and web frontends consume the same backend without custom logic.

sections.title: RESTful Order API in Spring Boot
When REST is the Right Choice
sections.content:
Use REST when you're building a **public-facing API** that external developers will consume—its predictability and standard HTTP semantics make documentation easier.

Choose REST for **mobile backends** where statelessness lets you scale horizontally as user count grows without sticky sessions. REST shines in **microservices architectures** where service-to-service communication benefits from uniform interfaces and HTTP's built-in features like caching headers. It's ideal when your data model maps naturally to **resources with CRUD operations**—User, Product, Invoice.

Avoid REST for real-time bidirectional communication (use WebSockets instead) or when you need ultra-low latency with binary protocols (consider gRPC).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating REST as a protocol**: Freshers often say "REST protocol" but it's an architectural style—a set of design principles, not a formal specification like SOAP or GraphQL. You can't be "REST compliant" because there's no standard body certifying APIs.
- **Ignoring statelessness**: Storing user session data in HttpSession breaks REST's core constraint. Every request should carry authentication (JWT token, API key) without server memory of previous interactions.
- **Using verbs in URIs**: Writing /getUser or /deleteOrder violates the uniform interface constraint—HTTP methods (GET, DELETE) already specify the action, so URIs should contain only nouns representing resources.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Architectural style**: REST is not a protocol or framework—it's a set of six constraints for designing scalable networked applications
**Resource-centric**: Everything is a resource with a unique URI—User, Order, Invoice—manipulated via standard HTTP methods
**Statelessness**: Each request contains all context (auth token, filters) without server-side session memory, enabling horizontal scaling
**Uniform interface**: Consistent patterns across all resources—GET retrieves, POST creates, PUT updates, DELETE removes
**HTTP semantics**: Leverage HTTP features—status codes (200, 404, 500), headers (Content-Type, Cache-Control), methods (GET is safe and idempotent)
**Client-server separation**: Frontend and backend evolve independently—mobile app and web UI consume the same REST API
**Roy Fielding**: REST was defined in Fielding's 2000 dissertation—understanding this origin shows depth beyond "it's JSON over HTTP"

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: REST is an architectural style for designing networked applications, not a protocol or framework. It's based on six constraints defined by Roy Fielding in his 2000 dissertation. An API is RESTful when it treats everything as a resource—like User, Order, or Invoice—and assigns each a unique URI. You use standard HTTP methods to operate on those resources. GET retrieves data, POST creates new resources, PUT updates existing ones, and DELETE removes them. The URI identifies what, the HTTP method specifies how. Statelessness is crucial. Each request carries all the information the server needs—authentication token, user context, filters—without relying on server-side session memory. This lets you scale horizontally because any server instance can handle any request without sticky sessions. A common mistake is calling REST a protocol or thinking stateless means no database. Databases are fine. What REST avoids is server session state. Another pitfall is using verbs in URIs like slash get user or slash delete order. HTTP methods already specify the action, so URIs should contain only nouns. In Spring Boot, you'd use the at-RestController annotation on your class and at-GetMapping or at-PostMapping on methods to map HTTP requests. The uniform interface constraint means your API is predictable—developers can guess how to interact with a new resource because all resources follow the same patterns. That's what makes REST powerful for public APIs and mobile backends.

question: What is a REST resource and how do you design URIs for it?
title: REST Resources and URI Design – Java Backend Interview
direct_answer: A REST resource is any entity or concept you can name and address—User, Order, Product, Invoice. URIs should use plural nouns for collections (slash users), singular identifiers for individual resources (slash users slash 42), and hierarchical paths for relationships (slash users slash 42 slash orders). HTTP methods determine the action, so URIs contain only nouns, never verbs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Your ability to design clean, predictable, maintainable REST APIs—a daily task in backend work
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using verbs in URIs like slash get user or slash delete order—this violates REST's uniform interface constraint
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between collection resources and singleton resources, and mention query parameters for filtering or pagination

sections.title: What Makes a Good REST Resource Design
sections.content:
A **REST resource** is any information or entity you can name and uniquely identify—User, Order, Product, Invoice, BlogPost, PaymentTransaction. Think of resources as nouns in your domain model.

The key insight is that resources aren't just database tables—they're abstractions. An Invoice resource might aggregate data from orders, line items, and tax calculations. **URI design** is how you address these resources. Good URIs are hierarchical, use plural nouns for collections, and reveal relationships without exposing implementation details. The pattern: /collection for all items, /collection/id for a specific item, /collection/id/subcollection for related items. For example, /users/42/orders retrieves all orders for user 42. The URI identifies the resource, the HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) defines the operation. This separation—what versus how—is central to REST's **uniform interface** constraint. Poor URI design makes your API unpredictable and hard to maintain.

sections.title: Resource URI Design in Spring Boot Controller
When to Apply These URI Patterns
sections.content:
Use **collection URIs** (/users, /products) when you need list operations with optional filtering via query parameters like /users?role=admin or /products?category=electronics. This pattern supports pagination naturally: /orders?page=2&size=20.

Use **singleton URIs** (/users/42, /orders/998) for operations on a specific resource—retrieve details, update fields, or delete.

Apply **hierarchical paths** (/users/42/orders, /orders/998/items) when expressing ownership or strong relationships—orders belonging to a user, line items within an order. This makes the relationship explicit in the URI structure.

Use **query parameters** for optional filters, sorting, or pagination—they don't change the resource identity.

Use **path segments** for required identifiers—/users/42 requires the user ID.

Avoid deep nesting beyond two levels—/users/42/orders/998/items/5/notes gets unwieldy. Instead, access /order-items/5/notes directly if the item ID is globally unique.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Verbs in URIs**: Writing /getUser or /deleteOrder violates REST principles because HTTP methods already define the action—use /users with GET or DELETE instead. The URI should identify the resource (what), not the operation (how).
- **Singular collection names**: Using /user instead of /users for a collection is inconsistent and confusing—readers expect /users to return multiple items and /users/42 to return one.
- **Exposing implementation**: URIs like /user-table or /get-user-by-id reveal database tables or method names—resources should represent domain concepts, not internal structure.
- **Deep nesting**: Paths like /organizations/1/departments/2/teams/3/users/4 become brittle when relationships change—if user 4 moves teams, the URI breaks. Keep nesting to two levels maximum.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Resource as noun**: A resource is any nameable entity—User, Order, Invoice—not tied to database tables but to domain concepts
**Plural collections**: Use /users for collections, /users/42 for individuals—consistency helps developers predict API behavior
**Hierarchical relationships**: Express ownership with nested paths like /users/42/orders, showing orders belonging to user 42
**No verbs in URIs**: The URI identifies the resource (what), HTTP method defines the operation (how)—use GET /users, not /getUsers
**Query parameters for filters**: Optional criteria go in query strings—/products?category=electronics&inStock=true—not in path segments
**Location header on create**: POST to /orders returns 201 Created with Location header pointing to /orders/123, the new resource URI
**Idempotency matters**: PUT to /users/42 replaces the entire user—calling it twice has the same effect as calling it once, unlike POST which creates duplicates

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A REST resource is any entity or concept you can name and address with a URI. Think User, Order, Product, Invoice—basically nouns from your domain model. Resources aren't just database tables. An Invoice resource might pull data from orders, line items, and tax calculations. It's an abstraction. For URI design, you use plural nouns for collections. So it's slash users, not slash user. For a specific resource, you add an identifier—slash users slash 42. If you need related resources, use hierarchical paths like slash users slash 42 slash orders. This shows that the orders belong to user 42. The key rule is that URIs contain only nouns, never verbs. HTTP methods already tell you the action. GET slash users retrieves the list. POST slash users creates a new user. DELETE slash users slash 42 removes user 42. A common mistake is writing slash get user or slash delete order. That's violating REST's uniform interface constraint. The URI identifies what, the method specifies how. Another pitfall is using singular names for collections. If you see slash user, does that mean all users or a specific one? It's ambiguous. Always use slash users for collections and slash users slash id for individuals. For filtering or pagination, use query parameters—slash products question mark category equals electronics. These are optional and don't change the resource identity. In Spring Boot, you use at-GetMapping with at-PathVariable to extract the ID from the URI and at-RequestParam to handle query strings. When you create a resource with POST, return status 201 Created and include a Location header pointing to the new resource URI. That's how clients discover where the new resource lives.

question: What is statelessness in REST and why does it matter?
title: Statelessness in REST APIs – Java Backend Interview
direct_answer: Statelessness means each HTTP request contains all information the server needs to process it—authentication token, user context, filters—without relying on server-side session memory. The server doesn't remember previous requests. This enables horizontal scaling because any server instance can handle any request without needing sticky sessions or session replication across nodes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the scalability implications of statelessness, not just the textbook definition
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking stateless means no database or no data persistence—databases are fine, server session state is what REST avoids
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect statelessness to horizontal scaling and explain how JWT tokens or API keys enable stateless authentication

sections.title: Why Statelessness Powers Scalable APIs
sections.content:
**Statelessness** is one of REST's six core constraints and arguably the most important for scalability. It means each HTTP request is a standalone transaction—it carries all the information the server needs to understand and process it, without depending on any context stored from previous requests. The server doesn't hold session data, shopping cart contents, or user preferences in memory between calls. Every detail—authentication token, user ID, pagination offset, sort order—arrives in the request headers, query parameters, or body.

Think of it like talking to someone with amnesia: you can't say "Remember what I asked five minutes ago?" You have to repeat all the context every time. The WHY is powerful: statelessness enables **horizontal scaling**. When you add more server instances behind a load balancer, any instance can handle any request. No sticky sessions, no session replication across nodes, no complex coordination. If server A crashes, server B picks up the next request without missing a beat because it doesn't rely on A's memory.

sections.title: Stateless Authentication with JWT in Spring Boot
When Statelessness is Critical
sections.content:
Embrace statelessness when building **APIs that need horizontal scaling**—as user count grows, you add server instances without complex session management. It's essential for **microservices architectures** where services communicate across network boundaries and session state doesn't naturally propagate.

Use stateless design for **mobile backends** because mobile apps naturally work in a stateless way—each request is independent, and the app stores user context locally.

Apply it in **public APIs** consumed by third parties who authenticate with API keys or OAuth tokens—these tokens carry identity without server sessions. Statelessness shines in **serverless or cloud-native deployments** where instances spin up and down dynamically. Consider stateful approaches (WebSockets, server-sent events) only for **real-time bidirectional communication** where the overhead of establishing connection state is amortized over many messages, or when you need **push notifications** from server to client without client polling.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing stateless with no persistence**: Freshers often think stateless means no database or no saved data. That's wrong. Databases store persistent state—User records, Order history—and that's fine. What REST avoids is server session state—data held in memory about ongoing client interactions. You can query the database in every request without violating statelessness.
- **Using HttpSession**: Storing user info in HttpSession breaks statelessness. When you do session-dot-set-attribute in Spring, you're tying the client to a specific server instance, requiring sticky sessions or session replication. Use JWT tokens or API keys in request headers instead.
- **Over-sending data**: Some freshers send entire user objects in every request to avoid sessions. Send only what's needed—a signed token with user ID and roles is enough. The server validates the token and fetches additional data from the database if required.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Self-contained requests**: Each request includes all context—authentication token, user ID, filters—without relying on server memory of past interactions
**No server-side sessions**: Avoid HttpSession or in-memory user state that ties clients to specific server instances
**Horizontal scaling**: Statelessness lets any server handle any request—add instances without sticky sessions or session replication
**JWT tokens**: A common stateless authentication pattern—the token contains user identity and claims, signed to prevent tampering
**Database persistence is fine**: Stateless doesn't mean no persistence—User records and Order history live in the database, queried per request
**Load balancer simplicity**: With stateless APIs, round-robin load balancing works perfectly—no need to route the same client to the same server
**Mobile-friendly**: Mobile apps naturally work statelessly—each API call is independent, and the app manages its own local state

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Statelessness means each HTTP request contains everything the server needs to process it. The server doesn't remember previous requests. If I ask for my order list, I have to send my authentication token in that request. If I ask for order details next, I send the token again. The server doesn't recall that I'm the same user from two seconds ago. It validates the token every time and extracts my user ID from it. This might sound inefficient, but it's actually what enables horizontal scaling. When you run multiple server instances behind a load balancer, any instance can handle any request because there's no session state tied to a specific server. If server A goes down, server B picks up the next request without issue. No sticky sessions, no session replication—just simple round-robin load balancing. A common mistake is thinking stateless means no database. That's not it. Databases are totally fine. What you avoid is server-side session state—like storing user info in HttpSession in Spring. That ties the client to one server instance. Instead, you use JWT tokens. The client sends the token in the Authorization header with every request. The token contains the user ID and roles, cryptographically signed so it can't be tampered with. The server validates the signature and extracts the claims. If it needs more data, it queries the database. Another pitfall is thinking you can't have any state at all. The client can maintain state—shopping cart in local storage, user preferences in the mobile app. The key is that the server doesn't hold conversational state between requests. Each request stands alone. This design is what makes REST APIs scale to millions of users across multiple data centers.

question: How does Spring Boot implement a REST API?
title: Implementing REST API in Spring Boot – Java Fresher Guide
direct_answer: Spring Boot implements REST APIs using annotations. At-RestController on the class marks it as a REST endpoint. At-GetMapping, at-PostMapping, at-PutMapping, at-DeleteMapping on methods map HTTP requests to handler methods. At-PathVariable extracts URI segments. At-RequestBody deserializes JSON into Java objects. ResponseEntity lets you return explicit HTTP status codes like 201 Created or 404 Not Found.

interviewer_intent.testing: Hands-on Spring Boot REST experience—can you write a working endpoint from scratch?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing at-Controller (returns view names for HTML) with at-RestController (returns JSON directly)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a complete CRUD example with proper status codes, and explain that at-RestController combines at-Controller and at-ResponseBody

sections.title: Spring Boot's Annotation-Driven REST Framework
sections.content:
**Spring Boot** makes building REST APIs straightforward through annotations that map HTTP requests to Java methods. The **at-RestController** annotation on a class tells Spring this is a REST endpoint that returns data (usually JSON) directly in the HTTP response body, not an HTML view.

It's a shorthand combining at-Controller and at-ResponseBody. Method-level annotations like **at-GetMapping**, **at-PostMapping**, **at-PutMapping**, **at-DeleteMapping** map specific HTTP methods to handler methods. **at-PathVariable** extracts values from URI segments like /users/{id}, binding them to method parameters. **at-RequestBody** deserializes incoming JSON from the request body into Java objects using Jackson. **ResponseEntity** wraps your response data with HTTP status codes and headers—you can return 200 OK, 201 Created, 404 Not Found, or 400 Bad Request explicitly. Behind the scenes, Spring Boot uses **Jackson** for JSON serialization and **Spring MVC** for request routing, but you rarely configure these directly—conventions and defaults handle most scenarios.

sections.title: Complete CRUD Controller in Spring Boot
When to Use These Spring Boot Patterns
sections.content:
Use **at-RestController** for any API endpoint that returns JSON or XML data to mobile apps, web frontends, or other services—it's the default choice for backend REST APIs.

Apply **ResponseEntity** when you need explicit control over HTTP status codes—201 Created after POST, 204 No Content after DELETE, 404 Not Found when a resource doesn't exist.

Use plain return types (List, Product) for simple cases where 200 OK is the only status—Spring wraps them automatically. Leverage **at-RequestParam** for optional filters or pagination—/products?category=electronics&page=2.

Use **at-PathVariable** for required resource identifiers in the URI—/products/42 where 42 is mandatory.

Apply **at-Valid** with at-RequestBody when you need input validation—Spring validates the incoming JSON against Bean Validation constraints like at-NotNull or at-Size.

Use **at-ExceptionHandler** methods in the controller to centralize error handling and return consistent error responses when validation fails or business rules are violated.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing at-Controller with at-RestController**: Using at-Controller without at-ResponseBody returns a view name (like "userList.html") instead of JSON. at-RestController is the shorthand that returns JSON directly—don't mix them unless you're building a hybrid app with both HTML pages and REST endpoints.
- **Ignoring HTTP status codes**: Returning the same 200 OK for everything makes debugging hard. Use 201 Created for POST, 204 No Content for DELETE, 404 Not Found when a resource doesn't exist, 400 Bad Request for validation errors. Clients rely on status codes to handle responses correctly.
- **Not validating input**: Accepting at-RequestBody without at-Valid lets invalid data reach your service layer. Add Bean Validation annotations (at-NotNull, at-Size) to your model and use at-Valid to trigger automatic validation.
- **Forgetting the Location header**: After creating a resource with POST, return ResponseEntity dot created with a Location header pointing to the new resource URI—this tells clients where to find what they just created.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **at-RestController**: Marks a class as a REST endpoint, combining at-Controller and at-ResponseBody to return JSON directly in the response
**HTTP method mappings**: at-GetMapping, at-PostMapping, at-PutMapping, at-DeleteMapping map HTTP verbs to Java methods—GET retrieves, POST creates, PUT updates, DELETE removes
**at-PathVariable**: Extracts URI segments like /products/{id} and binds them to method parameters—required resource identifiers
**at-RequestBody**: Deserializes JSON from the request body into Java objects using Jackson—used with POST and PUT
**ResponseEntity**: Wraps response data with explicit HTTP status codes and headers—201 Created, 404 Not Found, 204 No Content
**Constructor injection**: Prefer constructor-based dependency injection over at-Autowired fields—it's immutable and easier to test
**Jackson serialization**: Spring Boot uses Jackson by default to convert Java objects to JSON and vice versa—no manual configuration needed for common cases

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Spring Boot implements REST APIs using annotations that map HTTP requests to Java methods. You start by marking your class with at-RestController. This tells Spring it's a REST endpoint that returns JSON directly, not HTML views. It's actually a combination of at-Controller and at-ResponseBody, so you don't need to add at-ResponseBody on every method. Then you use method-level annotations like at-GetMapping, at-PostMapping, at-PutMapping, and at-DeleteMapping to map specific HTTP methods to your handler methods. For example, at-GetMapping on a method means it handles GET requests. If you need to extract values from the URI, you use at-PathVariable. So if your URI is slash products slash 42, you'd have at-PathVariable Long id in your method signature and Spring injects 42. For incoming JSON in the request body, you use at-RequestBody. Spring uses Jackson to deserialize the JSON into a Java object automatically. When you want to return specific HTTP status codes, you use ResponseEntity. Instead of just returning a Product object, you return ResponseEntity dot ok with the product for 200 OK, or ResponseEntity dot notFound dot build for 404 Not Found. After creating a resource with POST, you return 201 Created with a Location header pointing to the new resource. A common mistake is confusing at-Controller with at-RestController. at-Controller is for traditional Spring MVC apps that return HTML views. at-RestController is for REST APIs that return JSON. If you use at-Controller, you'd need to add at-ResponseBody on every method, which is tedious. Another pitfall is returning the same status code for everything. Use 201 Created after POST, 204 No Content after DELETE, and 404 Not Found when a resource doesn't exist. Clients rely on these codes to handle responses correctly. In a complete CRUD example, GET slash products retrieves the list, GET slash products slash id retrieves one product, POST slash products creates a new one, PUT slash products slash id updates it, and DELETE slash products slash id removes it. Each method returns the appropriate status code and uses ResponseEntity to control the HTTP response.

beats.text: Spring Boot implements REST through annotation-driven controllers. You annotate the class with @RestController to mark it as a REST endpoint, and annotate each method with the HTTP-method-specific mapping annotation to bind it to a URI and verb.

Before Spring Boot, REST controllers needed XML config and separate servlet setup. @RestController plus auto-configuration means zero XML — Spring Boot scans your classes and wires everything based on annotations.

items: @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody — return values are serialized to JSON, not treated as view names
@GetMapping/@PostMapping/@PutMapping/@DeleteMapping — bind the method to the matching HTTP verb and path
@PathVariable — extracts /tasks/{id} path segments into method parameters
@RequestBody — deserializes the JSON request body into a Java object using Jackson
ResponseEntity — lets you set the exact HTTP status code, headers, and body

beats.text: Task controller: @GetMapping returns List of TaskResponse (200). @PostMapping with @RequestBody TaskRequest returns ResponseEntity with status 201 CREATED and the saved body. @DeleteMapping with @PathVariable Long id returns ResponseEntity.noContent() for 204. In Spring Boot 3 with Java records you can use TaskRequest as an immutable request DTO directly with @RequestBody. production trap: @Controller without @ResponseBody returns a view name string — Spring tries to resolve it as a template and throws an error. Always use @RestController for JSON APIs.

items: Using @Controller instead of @RestController and wondering why Spring can't find the view template
Returning the JPA entity directly from @RestController — use a DTO to control what JSON gets exposed

speakable_v2.cap: @RestController + mapping annotations + @RequestBody + @PathVariable + ResponseEntity — these five pieces cover every CRUD endpoint you'll write.

question: What is the difference between a REST API and a web service?
title: REST API vs Web Service – Java Backend Interview
direct_answer: A web service is any software system accessible over a network—a broad category. REST API is one type of web service that uses HTTP with JSON. Other web service types include SOAP (XML over HTTP with strict contracts), gRPC (binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2), and GraphQL (query language over HTTP). REST dominates modern web APIs; SOAP persists in banking and enterprise; gRPC is for microservices.

interviewer_intent.testing: Your awareness of the API technology landscape beyond REST—not just vocabulary, but when to use what
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using 'web service' and 'REST API' as synonyms—REST is a subset of web services, not the only kind
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Briefly explain when you'd choose SOAP over REST (strict contracts, WS-Security) or gRPC over REST (low latency, microservices)

sections.title: Web Services as a Category and REST as One Implementation
sections.content:
**Web service** is the umbrella term for any programmatic interface accessible over a network—think of it as the category label. A **REST API** is one specific architectural style of web service that leverages HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and typically exchanges JSON.

But the web services world is broader: **SOAP** uses XML with rigid WSDL contracts and built-in security standards like WS-Security, making it the choice for banking and government systems that need formal agreements between parties. **gRPC** uses binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2 for high-performance microservice communication where milliseconds matter. **GraphQL** lets clients specify exactly what data they need in a single query, avoiding over-fetching. Each web service type emerged to solve different problems—REST won the public API battle because it's simple, stateless, and works beautifully with HTTP caching. But knowing when REST isn't the best tool shows depth.

sections.title: REST API vs Other Web Service Types
When to Choose Each Web Service Type
sections.content:
Use **REST** when building public-facing APIs for mobile apps or third-party integrations—it's the industry default, well-understood, and benefits from HTTP caching. Developers expect JSON over HTTP.

Use **SOAP** when you need formal contracts (WSDL), built-in security standards like WS-Security, or must integrate with legacy enterprise systems—banking APIs and government portals still heavily use SOAP because it enforces strict data validation and has mature tooling for transactions.

Use **gRPC** when you're building microservices that need sub-10ms latency and bidirectional streaming—the binary Protocol Buffers are 3-5x faster than JSON parsing, and HTTP/2 multiplexing reduces overhead.

Use **GraphQL** when your frontend team needs flexibility to fetch nested data in one request—mobile apps benefit from reducing round-trips, though you trade REST's simplicity for query complexity.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating REST and web service as synonyms**: Many freshers say 'I built a web service' when they mean 'I built a REST API.' Web service is the category; REST is one implementation. This shows confusion about the landscape.
- **Dismissing SOAP as outdated**: While REST dominates new projects, SOAP isn't dead—banks, insurance companies, and government agencies use it for inter-system communication where formal contracts and transaction support matter. Saying 'SOAP is legacy' in an enterprise interview can backfire.
- **Not knowing when JSON hurts performance**: For high-frequency microservice calls (thousands per second), JSON parsing overhead adds up. gRPC's binary format is measurably faster, but freshers often default to REST without considering latency requirements.

sections.title: Spring Boot Example
Key Points
content: **Web service**: any network-accessible software interface—REST, SOAP, gRPC, GraphQL are all web services
**REST API**: web service using HTTP methods and JSON, stateless, dominates public APIs and mobile backends
**SOAP**: XML-based web service with WSDL contracts, used in banking and enterprise for strict validation and security
**gRPC**: binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2, fastest option for microservices needing low latency and streaming
**GraphQL**: query-based web service letting clients specify data shape, reduces over-fetching for complex frontends
**WSDL**: Web Services Description Language, the contract format SOAP requires to define operations and data types
**HTTP/2**: protocol that gRPC uses for multiplexing and header compression, making it faster than REST on HTTP/1.1

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: So a web service is really just the broad category—any software you can call over a network to get data or trigger actions. A REST API is one specific type of web service, and it's the one we use most often today because it's simple. REST uses HTTP methods like GET and POST, and usually returns JSON. But there are other web service types that solve different problems. SOAP is another one—it uses XML instead of JSON and requires a formal contract called a WSDL. You still see SOAP in banking and government systems because it has built-in security standards like WS-Security, and the contract enforcement prevents breaking changes. Then there's gRPC, which uses binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2. It's way faster than REST, so you'd use it for microservices that need really low latency—think internal service-to-service calls where milliseconds matter. And GraphQL is another type where the client can ask for exactly the data it needs in one query, which is great for mobile apps that don't want to make five REST calls to build one screen. The key thing is REST isn't a synonym for web service—it's one approach. In a Spring Boot project serving a mobile client, REST is the default choice because it's well-supported, cacheable, and easy to debug. But if you were building a payment gateway integration, you might have to call a SOAP service. Or if you're doing inter-service communication in a microservices setup with strict latency requirements, you'd consider gRPC. Understanding when REST isn't the best tool shows you're thinking beyond the tutorial level.

groups.label: Web service
groups.text: An umbrella term for any service reachable over a network via a standard protocol. REST, SOAP, gRPC, and GraphQL are all types of web service.

groups.label: REST API
groups.text: A web service that follows REST constraints — resources with URIs, standard HTTP methods, stateless, JSON responses. Dominant for web and mobile today.

items: REST: new web or mobile API — lightweight, tooling everywhere, JSON native
SOAP: integrating with a legacy bank or insurance system that already has a WSDL
gRPC: internal microservice calls where binary speed and strong typing matter

beats.text: Our task app uses REST — GET /tasks over HTTP returning JSON. If we were integrating with a bank's payment gateway from 2010, we'd likely consume a SOAP endpoint with a WSDL. If task-service needed to call notification-service at high volume internally, gRPC would be faster than REST. candidates miss: the question says REST vs web service, not REST vs SOAP. The key point is that web service is the parent category — REST is one option under it.

speakable_v2.cap: Web service = umbrella. REST is the most common type — HTTP + JSON + stateless. SOAP for enterprise contracts, gRPC for internal speed.
